article.title: How to Weatherstrip an Exterior Door
article.summary: Stop drafts around an exterior door: find the leaks, replace kerf-in weatherstripping or add new seals, and adjust the sweep for a tight close.
article.body:
Even a gap of 1/8 in around an exterior door lets in a surprising amount of air. New weatherstripping is one of the cheapest energy upgrades you can make, and it also cuts noise, dust and bugs. This guide covers a standard hinged entry door.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: wear gloves when cutting metal-backed weatherstrip, because cut edges are sharp. If you lift the door off its hinges, have a helper. Exterior doors are heavy.

Steps

  1. Find where the air gets in

    On a cold or windy day, run your hand around the closed door's edges. At night, have a helper shine a flashlight around the perimeter from outside while you look for light from inside. Close the door on a sheet of paper in several spots: if it slides out easily, the seal there is too weak.

    Done right: you've marked the leaky zones, usually the latch side, the top corners and the bottom.

  2. Identify your weatherstrip type

    Look at the doorstop, the molding the door closes against. Most modern doors have a slot (kerf) with a foam or rubber strip pressed into it. Older doors may have nailed-on strips or none at all. Buy the matching type.

    Done right: you know whether you need kerf-in strip or surface-mounted seals.

  3. Remove the old weatherstrip

    Kerf-in strip pulls straight out: grab the end and peel it along its length. For adhesive foam, scrape it off with a putty knife and clean the residue with rubbing alcohol.

    Done right: the groove or stop is clean and dry along its whole length.

  4. Install the new strip on the head, then the sides

    Cut the top piece to fit between the side jambs and press it in. Then run each side piece from the top down, cutting it to length at the floor. Push kerf-in strip in with your thumb, not a tool, so you don't tear the flange.

    Done right: the strip is continuous, with tight corners and no gaps or stretched sections.

  5. Seal the bottom

    Check the door sweep or threshold seal. Replace a torn sweep, then adjust it so it brushes the threshold lightly. Many thresholds also have adjustment screws that raise them to meet the door.

    Done right: no light shows under the door, and it still opens without dragging.

  6. Test the close and adjust

    New weatherstrip is thicker than worn-out strip, so the door may need a firmer push to latch for the first few days. If it won't latch at all, adjust the strike plate slightly outward. Repeat the paper test.

    Done right: the door latches with a normal push, and the paper is gripped firmly everywhere.

Call a pro if: the door is warped, the frame is rotted (soft wood near the bottom of the jambs), or there's a gap you can see even with new seals. Those need frame repair or a door adjustment, not just weatherstripping.

FAQ

How do I know if my door needs new weatherstripping?

Drafts you can feel, light visible around the edges, a sheet of paper that slides out when the door is closed on it, or strips that are flattened, cracked or missing.

What's the best weatherstripping for an exterior door?

If your frame has a kerf slot, use the matching kerf-in foam or silicone. It's the most durable option. Adhesive foam works on doors without a slot but wears faster.

Why won't my door close after new weatherstripping?

New seals are fuller than old ones. Give them a few days to compress, or move the strike plate slightly.

How often should door weatherstripping be replaced?

Inspect it every fall. Most strips last a few years before they flatten or crack.
